fields.Question: What is the time complexity of reading the element at index i of an array?
fields.Hint: The address can be computed directly from the index.
fields.Fact: Array elements sit in contiguous memory, so element i lives at base address plus i times the element size.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the worst case time to search for a value in an unsorted array of n elements?
fields.Hint: Without order, nothing lets you skip elements.
fields.Fact: Linear search is optimal for unsorted data, since any unexamined element could be the target.

fields.Question: What is the time complexity of inserting at the front of a dynamic array of n elements?
fields.Hint: Think about what happens to the existing elements.
fields.Fact: Every existing element has to shift one position to make room.

fields.Text: Appending to a dynamic array costs {{c1::O(1)}} amortized time when the capacity grows {{c2::geometrically}}, for example by doubling.
fields.Extra: Growing by a fixed constant amount instead would make n appends cost O(n^2) in total.
fields.Hint: Total copying stays proportional to n if each resize multiplies the capacity.
fields.Fact: CPython lists over-allocate when they grow so that repeated appends stay amortized constant time.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: Big O gives an asymptotic {{c1::upper}} bound, Big Omega gives a {{c2::lower}} bound, and Big Theta gives a {{c3::tight}} bound.
fields.Extra: f(n) = Theta(g(n)) means f is both O(g(n)) and Omega(g(n)).
fields.Hint: Theta is the one that pins the growth rate from both sides.
fields.Fact: Big O notation was popularized in computer science by Donald Knuth, who also advocated Omega and Theta in a 1976 letter.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the time complexity of two nested loops that each run n times with O(1) work inside?
fields.Hint: Multiply the iteration counts.
fields.Fact: Doubling n makes a quadratic algorithm roughly four times slower.

fields.Text: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n) solves to {{c1::Theta(n log n)}}.
fields.Extra: This is the recurrence of merge sort.
fields.Hint: Each of the log n levels of the recursion tree does linear work in total.
fields.Fact: The master theorem handles this as the case where the work is spread evenly across levels.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What does the recurrence T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) solve to?
fields.Hint: Count how many times n can be halved before reaching 1.
fields.Fact: This is the recurrence of binary search.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: Amortized analysis bounds the {{c1::average cost per operation over a worst case sequence}} of operations, without relying on probability.
fields.Extra: Common methods are aggregate analysis, the accounting method and the potential method.
fields.Hint: It differs from average case analysis, which assumes a distribution of inputs.
fields.Fact: CLRS presents three amortized techniques: aggregate, accounting and potential.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Hint: Think of an algorithm that halves the problem each step.
fields.Fact: With n around one billion, log base 2 of n is only about 30.

fields.Hint: Efficient comparison sorts land here.
fields.Fact: Comparison sorting cannot beat this bound in the worst case.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Hint: The cost does not depend on the input size.
fields.Fact: Constant time does not mean fast, only that the cost is bounded independent of n.

fields.Question: What is the time complexity of inserting a node at the head of a singly linked list?
fields.Hint: Only a couple of pointers change.
fields.Fact: No elements move, which is the main advantage of linked lists over arrays for insertion.

fields.Question: What is the time complexity of accessing the k-th element of a singly linked list of n nodes, in the worst case?
fields.Hint: There is no index arithmetic, only next pointers.
fields.Fact: Linked lists trade random access for cheap insertion and deletion at known positions.

fields.Question: Given a pointer to a node in a doubly linked list, what is the time to delete that node?
fields.Hint: The node already knows both of its neighbours.
fields.Fact: In a singly linked list you would need the previous node, which may require a scan.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: How much extra space does reversing a singly linked list iteratively need?
fields.Hint: You only need a few pointer variables.
fields.Fact: The recursive version uses O(n) stack space instead.

fields.Question: Which kind of linked list lets you traverse forward and backward from any node?
fields.Hint: Each node stores two links.
fields.Fact: Java's LinkedList is a doubly linked list.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: Floyd's cycle detection moves a {{c1::slow}} pointer one step and a {{c2::fast}} pointer two steps; they meet if and only if the list has a cycle.
fields.Extra: Runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space.
fields.Hint: Picture two runners on a circular track.
fields.Fact: It is also known as the tortoise and hare algorithm.

fields.Question: In what order does a stack remove elements?
fields.Hint: Think of a pile of plates.
fields.Fact: The call stack that tracks function calls follows this order.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: In what order does a queue remove elements?
fields.Hint: Think of a line at a ticket counter.
fields.Fact: Breadth first search relies on this order to visit vertices level by level.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Which data structure is the standard choice for checking that brackets are balanced?
fields.Hint: The most recently opened bracket must close first.
fields.Fact: The same idea underlies parsing expressions in compilers.

fields.Question: Which Python standard library type supports O(1) appends and pops at both ends?
fields.Hint: It lives in the collections module.
fields.Fact: Indexing into the middle of this type is O(n), unlike a list.

fields.Question: In CPython, what is the time complexity of list.pop(0) on a list of n elements?
fields.Hint: Remember how lists are stored.
fields.Fact: Popping from the end with list.pop() is O(1), so lists make poor queues.

fields.Question: What does deque stand for?
fields.Hint: It describes where you can add and remove.
fields.Fact: It is usually pronounced like deck.

fields.Text: A {{c1::circular buffer}} implements a fixed capacity queue in an array by wrapping the head and tail indices modulo the capacity.
fields.Extra: Also called a ring buffer.
fields.Hint: The end of the array connects back to its start.
fields.Fact: Ring buffers are common in audio and network drivers because they never reallocate.

fields.Text: A queue can be built from {{c1::two}} stacks with amortized O(1) time per operation.
fields.Extra: One stack receives pushes; the other is refilled only when empty.
fields.Hint: Each element is moved between stacks at most once.
fields.Fact: This is a classic exercise in amortized analysis.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the time complexity of push and pop on an array-backed stack, amortized?
fields.Hint: Both happen at the same end.
fields.Fact: An occasional resize is paid for by the many cheap operations around it.

fields.Question: What is the expected time of a lookup in a hash table with a good hash function and bounded load factor?
fields.Hint: Hashing jumps straight to a bucket.
fields.Fact: This expectation assumes keys hash roughly uniformly across buckets.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the worst case time of a lookup in a hash table with separate chaining and n keys?
fields.Hint: Imagine every key landing in the same bucket.
fields.Fact: Adversarial inputs that force collisions are the basis of hash flooding attacks.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: The load factor of a hash table is {{c1::the number of stored entries divided by the number of buckets}}.
fields.Extra: Tables usually resize when it passes a threshold.
fields.Hint: It measures how full the table is.
fields.Fact: In separate chaining, the load factor equals the average chain length.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the collision resolution strategy that keeps a list of entries in each bucket?
fields.Hint: Colliding entries are linked together.
fields.Fact: With chaining the load factor can exceed 1.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the collision resolution strategy that stores every entry in the table array itself and probes other slots on collision?
fields.Hint: No external lists are used.
fields.Fact: The load factor of an open addressed table can never exceed 1.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Which open addressing scheme probes slots h, h+1, h+2 and so on?
fields.Hint: The step between probes is constant.
fields.Fact: Its sequential access pattern is cache friendly despite clustering.

fields.Text: Linear probing suffers from {{c1::primary clustering}}, where long runs of occupied slots grow and slow down inserts and searches.
fields.Extra: Quadratic probing and double hashing reduce it.
fields.Hint: Occupied slots tend to clump together.
fields.Fact: Knuth analyzed linear probing in 1963, one of the first analyses of an algorithm's average performance.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Which open addressing scheme uses a second hash function to choose the probe step?
fields.Hint: The step size depends on the key.
fields.Fact: Different keys that collide at first usually follow different probe sequences.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the default load factor of java.util.HashMap?
fields.Hint: It is a fraction between one half and one.
fields.Fact: The Javadoc describes this value as a good tradeoff between time and space costs.

fields.Text: In OpenJDK 8 and later, a HashMap bucket with many collisions can be converted from a linked list to a {{c1::balanced tree}}, improving worst case lookups in that bucket.
fields.Extra: The conversion threshold in the OpenJDK source is 8 entries per bin.
fields.Hint: Think about what structure keeps search logarithmic.
fields.Fact: This was added to limit the damage of many keys colliding in one bucket.

fields.Question: Since Python 3.7, in what order does iterating a dict yield its keys?
fields.Hint: It is not sorted order.
fields.Fact: The ordering was an implementation detail in CPython 3.6 and became a language guarantee in 3.7.

fields.Text: A hash table does not keep keys in order, so finding the {{c1::smallest key}} or iterating in sorted order needs a different structure such as a balanced BST.
fields.Extra: Ordered operations are the main reason to pick a tree map over a hash map.
fields.Hint: Hashing scatters keys deliberately.
fields.Fact: Java offers both: HashMap for speed and TreeMap for ordered keys.

fields.Question: What is the time complexity of reading the minimum of a binary min-heap?
fields.Hint: Where does the smallest element live?
fields.Fact: The minimum is always at the root, index 0 in the array form.

fields.Question: What is the worst case time of inserting into a binary heap of n elements?
fields.Hint: The new element bubbles up along one path.
fields.Fact: A binary heap is a complete tree, so its height is about log2 n.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the worst case time of removing the minimum from a binary min-heap of n elements?
fields.Hint: The last element moves to the root and sifts down.
fields.Fact: Python's heapq.heappop does exactly this.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the time complexity of building a binary heap from n unordered elements with bottom up heapify?
fields.Hint: Most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a little.
fields.Fact: It is better than the O(n log n) of inserting the elements one by one.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: In a 0-indexed array binary heap, the children of index i are at {{c1::2i + 1}} and {{c2::2i + 2}}, and its parent is at {{c3::(i - 1) // 2}}.
fields.Extra: With 1-based indexing the children are 2i and 2i + 1, and the parent is i // 2.
fields.Hint: Each level doubles the number of nodes.
fields.Fact: Python's heapq uses 0-based indexing, while CLRS uses 1-based.

fields.Question: Is Python's heapq a min-heap or a max-heap?
fields.Hint: heap[0] is the answer to a common question.
fields.Fact: A common workaround for max-heap behaviour is pushing negated keys.

fields.Question: To track the k-th largest element of a stream, which heap do you maintain?
fields.Aliases:
min heap of size k
min-heap
fields.Hint: The root should be the weakest of the current top k.
fields.Fact: Each new element costs O(log k).

fields.Text: In a max-heap, every node's key is {{c1::greater than or equal to}} the keys of its children.
fields.Extra: So the maximum is at the root.
fields.Hint: Compare a parent with its children.
fields.Fact: Siblings in a heap have no required order between them.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: A binary heap is a {{c1::complete}} binary tree, which lets it be stored in an array with no pointers.
fields.Extra: Every level is full except possibly the last, which fills from the left.
fields.Hint: Think about why there are no gaps in the array.
fields.Fact: This shape guarantees the height is floor(log2 n).
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the amortized time of decrease-key in a Fibonacci heap?
fields.Hint: It is cheaper than in a binary heap.
fields.Fact: This bound gives Dijkstra's algorithm O(E + V log V) time.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Merging k sorted lists with N total elements using a min-heap takes what time?
fields.Hint: The heap holds one candidate per list.
fields.Fact: Each of the N elements is pushed and popped once in a heap of size at most k.

fields.Question: What is the worst case search time in a balanced binary search tree with n keys?
fields.Hint: Height controls the cost.
fields.Fact: Balanced trees such as AVL and red-black trees keep the height O(log n).
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the worst case search time in an unbalanced binary search tree with n keys?
fields.Hint: Insert sorted keys and look at the shape.
fields.Fact: Inserting keys in sorted order makes a plain BST degenerate into a linked list.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What does an inorder traversal of a binary search tree produce?
fields.Aliases:
sorted order
ascending order
sorted keys
fields.Hint: Left subtree, node, right subtree.
fields.Fact: This makes inorder traversal a quick way to validate a BST.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Hint: The node sits in the middle.
fields.Fact: On a BST this order is ascending.

fields.Hint: The node comes first.
fields.Fact: Preorder is a natural way to copy or serialize a tree.

fields.Hint: The node comes last.
fields.Fact: Postorder suits deleting a tree, since children are handled before their parent.

fields.Question: Which data structure does a level order traversal of a tree use?
fields.Hint: Nodes are visited in the order they are discovered.
fields.Fact: Level order traversal is breadth first search on a tree.

fields.Text: In an AVL tree, the heights of the two child subtrees of every node differ by {{c1::at most one}}.
fields.Extra: Rotations restore this after inserts and deletes.
fields.Hint: The balance factor is small.
fields.Fact: This keeps the height at most roughly 1.44 log2 n.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: The AVL tree is named after which inventors?
fields.Aliases:
Adelson-Velsky, Landis
Adelson Velsky and Landis
fields.Hint: Two Soviet mathematicians, 1962.
fields.Fact: The AVL tree is generally considered the first self-balancing binary search tree.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: After inserting into an AVL tree, at most {{c1::one single or double rotation}} is needed to restore balance.
fields.Extra: Deletion can need rotations at many levels.
fields.Hint: Fixing the lowest unbalanced ancestor restores its old height.
fields.Fact: A double rotation is two single rotations performed in sequence.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: In a red-black tree, a red node never has a {{c1::red}} child, and every path from a node down to its descendant leaves contains the same number of {{c2::black}} nodes.
fields.Extra: The root is black, and leaves (NIL) are black.
fields.Hint: Two colors, two rules to remember.
fields.Fact: Red-black trees were described by Guibas and Sedgewick in 1978, building on Bayer's symmetric binary B-trees.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: A red-black tree with n internal nodes has height at most {{c1::2 log2(n + 1)}}.
fields.Extra: So search, insert and delete are O(log n).
fields.Hint: It is within a constant factor of the optimal height.
fields.Fact: No root to leaf path is more than twice as long as any other.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Which is more strictly balanced, an AVL tree or a red-black tree?
fields.Hint: Compare their height bounds.
fields.Fact: Stricter balance tends to make AVL lookups slightly faster, while red-black trees usually do less rebalancing work on updates.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: java.util.TreeMap is based on which data structure?
fields.Hint: The Javadoc names it directly.
fields.Fact: TreeMap guarantees log n time for containsKey, get, put and remove.

fields.Text: B-trees are designed for storage that reads and writes in large {{c1::blocks}}, such as disks, which is why they are widely used in databases and file systems.
fields.Extra: Each node holds many keys, so the tree is very shallow.
fields.Hint: A high branching factor means few node reads per lookup.
fields.Fact: Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight introduced B-trees in 1970 at Boeing.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: In a B-tree, all leaves are at the {{c1::same depth}}.
fields.Extra: The tree grows in height only by splitting the root.
fields.Hint: Balance is perfect in one specific sense.
fields.Fact: Growth at the root rather than the leaves is what keeps every leaf level.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: In a B+ tree, where are the data records or record pointers stored?
fields.Aliases:
leaves
leaf nodes
only in the leaves
fields.Hint: Internal nodes only guide the search.
fields.Fact: Leaves are typically linked, which makes range scans efficient.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Hint: It is great for autocomplete.
fields.Fact: The name comes from retrieval; Edward Fredkin coined it in 1960.

fields.Question: What is the time to look up a key of length m in a trie, independent of the number of keys stored?
fields.Hint: Follow one edge per character.
fields.Fact: Unlike a hash table, a trie also supports prefix queries naturally.

fields.Question: What is the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height h, where a single root has height 0?
fields.Hint: Sum the nodes per level: 1, 2, 4, and so on.
fields.Fact: A tree that reaches this bound is called a perfect binary tree.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: In a BST, the lowest common ancestor of keys p and q is the first node on the path from the root whose key lies {{c1::between p and q}} (inclusive).
fields.Extra: If both keys are smaller, go left; if both are larger, go right.
fields.Hint: Where do the search paths for p and q split?
fields.Fact: This runs in O(h) time, where h is the tree height.

fields.Text: To validate a BST it is not enough to compare each node with its children; each node must lie within {{c1::bounds inherited from its ancestors}}.
fields.Extra: Equivalently, an inorder traversal must be strictly increasing (when keys are distinct).
fields.Hint: A node deep in a left subtree can still violate the root.
fields.Fact: This is one of the most common mistakes in BST interview questions.

fields.Question: What is the time of a range query on a segment tree over n elements?
fields.Hint: A query touches only a few nodes per level.
fields.Fact: Segment trees also support point updates in O(log n).

fields.Hint: It is the compact alternative to a segment tree for prefix sums.
fields.Fact: Peter Fenwick described it in 1994 for cumulative frequency tables.

fields.Text: To delete a BST node with two children, replace it with its inorder {{c1::successor}} (or predecessor) and delete that node instead.
fields.Extra: The successor is the minimum of the right subtree.
fields.Hint: Which key could take its place without breaking order?
fields.Fact: The successor has at most one child, so its removal is simple.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Which self-adjusting BST moves each accessed node to the root?
fields.Hint: The operation is named after spreading out.
fields.Fact: Sleator and Tarjan introduced it in 1985 with O(log n) amortized bounds.

fields.Question: Which data structure does breadth first search use to hold the frontier?
fields.Hint: Discovered vertices wait their turn.
fields.Fact: BFS explores vertices in order of their distance in edges from the source.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Which data structure does an iterative depth first search use?
fields.Hint: The recursive version uses the call stack.
fields.Fact: Swapping one data structure for another turns DFS into BFS.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the time complexity of BFS or DFS on a graph stored as adjacency lists?
fields.Hint: Each vertex and each edge is handled a constant number of times.
fields.Fact: On an adjacency matrix the same traversal costs O(V^2).
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: How much space does an adjacency matrix use for a graph with V vertices?
fields.Hint: One cell per ordered pair of vertices.
fields.Fact: Matrices allow O(1) edge checks, which helps for dense graphs.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: How much space do adjacency lists use for a graph with V vertices and E edges?
fields.Hint: Count the list heads and the list entries.
fields.Fact: Adjacency lists are the usual choice for sparse graphs.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Which algorithm finds shortest paths by edge count in an unweighted graph in O(V + E)?
fields.Hint: Explore level by level.
fields.Fact: BFS is effectively Dijkstra's algorithm when every edge weight is 1.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Dijkstra's algorithm can give wrong answers when the graph has what?
fields.Hint: It assumes a finalized vertex never gets cheaper.
fields.Fact: Bellman-Ford handles this case and can also detect negative cycles.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the running time of Dijkstra's algorithm with a binary heap?
fields.Aliases:
O((V+E) log V)
O(E log V)
fields.Hint: Every edge may trigger a heap operation.
fields.Fact: With a Fibonacci heap the bound improves to O(E + V log V).
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Which single source shortest path algorithm allows negative edge weights and detects negative cycles?
fields.Hint: It relaxes every edge V - 1 times.
fields.Fact: If any edge can still be relaxed after V - 1 rounds, a negative cycle is reachable.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the running time of the Bellman-Ford algorithm?
fields.Hint: Count rounds times edges per round.
fields.Fact: It is slower than Dijkstra but handles negative weights.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Which dynamic programming algorithm computes all pairs shortest paths in O(V^3)?
fields.Hint: Three nested loops over vertices.
fields.Fact: The outermost loop must range over the intermediate vertex.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: A* search returns an optimal path when its heuristic is {{c1::admissible}}, meaning it never overestimates the true remaining cost.
fields.Extra: On graph search without reopening nodes, the stronger consistent property is used.
fields.Hint: The guess must be optimistic.
fields.Fact: With a heuristic of zero everywhere, A* behaves like Dijkstra's algorithm.

fields.Text: Shortest paths in a weighted DAG, even with negative weights, can be found in O(V + E) by relaxing edges in {{c1::topological order}}.
fields.Extra: No priority queue is needed.
fields.Hint: Process each vertex after all its predecessors.
fields.Fact: The same technique finds longest paths in a DAG by negating weights.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: In 0-1 BFS, for graphs with edge weights of only 0 or 1, which data structure replaces the priority queue?
fields.Hint: Zero-weight edges go to one end, one-weight edges to the other.
fields.Fact: It runs in O(V + E), faster than Dijkstra with a heap.

fields.Question: Which data structure does Kruskal's algorithm use to check whether an edge would form a cycle?
fields.Aliases:
disjoint set union
DSU
disjoint-set
disjoint set
fields.Hint: It tracks which vertices are already connected.
fields.Fact: Kruskal considers edges in increasing order of weight.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: Prim's algorithm grows a single tree from a start vertex, repeatedly adding the {{c1::lightest edge}} connecting the tree to a vertex outside it.
fields.Extra: A priority queue keyed by edge weight makes it efficient.
fields.Hint: Compare with Kruskal, which grows a forest.
fields.Fact: Prim's algorithm was discovered earlier by Vojtech Jarnik in 1930.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the running time of Kruskal's algorithm, dominated by sorting the edges?
fields.Aliases:
O(E log V)
E log E
fields.Hint: Sorting is the expensive step.
fields.Fact: O(E log E) and O(E log V) are equal asymptotically, since E is at most V^2.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: Cut property: for any cut of a connected weighted graph, a {{c1::minimum weight}} edge crossing the cut belongs to some minimum spanning tree.
fields.Extra: Both Kruskal and Prim are justified by it.
fields.Hint: Any spanning tree must cross the cut somewhere.
fields.Fact: If edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: How many edges does a spanning tree of a connected graph with V vertices have?
fields.Hint: A tree on k nodes is connected and has no cycles.
fields.Fact: Adding any further edge to a spanning tree creates exactly one cycle.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: A topological ordering of a directed graph exists exactly when the graph is what?
fields.Hint: Think of course prerequisites.
fields.Fact: A cycle would require some vertex to come before itself.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Kahn's algorithm for topological sorting repeatedly removes vertices with what property?
fields.Aliases:
in-degree 0
indegree 0
no incoming edges
zero in-degree
fields.Hint: These vertices have no remaining prerequisites.
fields.Fact: If vertices remain when no candidate exists, the graph has a cycle.

fields.Text: Reversing the DFS {{c1::postorder}} (order of finishing times) of a DAG yields a topological order.
fields.Extra: A vertex finishes only after everything reachable from it.
fields.Hint: Think about when DFS is done with a vertex.
fields.Fact: CLRS sorts vertices by decreasing finishing time, which is the same thing.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: A directed graph has a cycle if and only if DFS finds a {{c1::back}} edge.
fields.Extra: Such an edge points to a vertex still on the recursion stack.
fields.Hint: Track vertices that are in progress, not just visited.
fields.Fact: The three color scheme of white, gray and black makes this check easy.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Name a linear time algorithm for finding strongly connected components.
fields.Hint: One uses low-link values, another uses two DFS passes.
fields.Fact: Contracting each strongly connected component gives a DAG.

fields.Text: A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no cycle of {{c1::odd}} length.
fields.Extra: Check by 2-coloring with BFS or DFS.
fields.Hint: Try coloring a triangle with two colors.
fields.Fact: Every tree is bipartite.

fields.Hint: Greedy, with a priority queue.
fields.Fact: Dijkstra said he designed it in about twenty minutes without pencil and paper.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Hint: Three nested loops over vertices.
fields.Fact: It works with negative edges as long as there are no negative cycles.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: With path compression and union by rank, what is the amortized time per union-find operation?
fields.Hint: It grows so slowly it is effectively constant.
fields.Fact: Robert Tarjan proved this inverse Ackermann bound in 1975.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: The two standard union-find optimizations are {{c1::path compression}} and {{c2::union by rank}} (or by size).
fields.Extra:
def find(x):
    if parent[x] != x:
        parent[x] = find(parent[x])
    return parent[x]
fields.Hint: One flattens trees during find, the other keeps them shallow during union.
fields.Fact: Union by rank alone already keeps every tree at height O(log n).

fields.Text: In an undirected graph, adding edge (u, v) creates a cycle if find(u) and find(v) return the {{c1::same root}}.
fields.Extra: This is the check Kruskal's algorithm uses.
fields.Hint: Are the endpoints already connected?
fields.Fact: Union-find only supports adding connections, not removing them.

fields.Text: After processing all edges with union-find, the number of connected components equals the number of {{c1::roots}}, that is elements whose parent is themselves.
fields.Extra: Start with n components and subtract one per successful union.
fields.Hint: Each set has one representative.
fields.Fact: Union-find is also called a disjoint set forest.

fields.Text: Adjacency lists suit {{c1::sparse}} graphs, while an adjacency matrix suits {{c2::dense}} graphs or frequent edge lookups.
fields.Extra: Sparse means E is much smaller than V^2.
fields.Hint: Compare memory use with the number of edges.
fields.Fact: Many real world graphs such as road networks are sparse.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the worst case time of merge sort?
fields.Hint: Halve, recurse, merge in linear time.
fields.Fact: John von Neumann described merge sort in 1945.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the worst case time of quicksort?
fields.Hint: Imagine always picking the smallest element as pivot.
fields.Fact: A naive first-element pivot hits the worst case on already sorted input.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the expected time of randomized quicksort?
fields.Hint: Random pivots split well on average.
fields.Fact: Tony Hoare developed quicksort around 1959 to 1960.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the worst case time of heapsort?
fields.Hint: Build a heap, then extract n times.
fields.Fact: Heapsort sorts in place with O(1) extra space.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the time of insertion sort on input that is already sorted?
fields.Hint: Each element is compared once and stays put.
fields.Fact: Its running time is O(n + d), where d is the number of inversions.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: How much auxiliary space does a standard array merge sort use?
fields.Hint: The merge step needs somewhere to put the output.
fields.Fact: Merge sort on linked lists can avoid the extra array.

fields.Text: A sorting algorithm is stable if {{c1::elements with equal keys keep their original relative order}}.
fields.Extra: Stability lets you sort by one key, then another, and keep the first ordering among ties.
fields.Hint: Think about records that compare equal.
fields.Fact: Python guarantees that its built-in sort is stable.

fields.Question: Which classic O(n log n) worst case comparison sort is stable?
fields.Hint: It merges by taking from the left run on ties.
fields.Fact: Heapsort and typical in-place quicksort are not stable.

fields.Question: Which in-place O(n log n) worst case sort is not stable?
fields.Hint: It moves the root to the end repeatedly.
fields.Fact: Long distance swaps during sifting reorder equal keys.

fields.Question: Which algorithm does Java's Arrays.sort use for arrays of primitives such as int[]?
fields.Hint: It uses two pivots, not one.
fields.Fact: Arrays.sort for object arrays uses a stable merge sort instead.

fields.Question: Which C++ standard library function guarantees a stable sort?
fields.Hint: std::sort does not make this promise.
fields.Fact: std::sort is required to run in O(n log n) comparisons since C++11.

fields.Question: What is the worst case lower bound on comparisons for any comparison based sort of n elements?
fields.Aliases:
Ω(n log n)
n log n
fields.Hint: A decision tree needs a leaf for every permutation.
fields.Fact: log2(n!) is about n log2 n, which gives the bound.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the running time of counting sort on n integers in the range 0 to k?
fields.Hint: It never compares elements.
fields.Fact: It beats the comparison lower bound because it uses keys as array indices.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: LSD radix sort processes digits from least to most significant and requires the per-digit sort to be {{c1::stable}}.
fields.Extra: Counting sort is the usual per-digit sort.
fields.Hint: Earlier passes must not be undone by later ones.
fields.Fact: Herman Hollerith's tabulating machines of the 1890s used a form of radix sorting on punched cards.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Which quicksort partition scheme moves two indices toward each other from both ends?
fields.Hint: Named after the inventor of quicksort.
fields.Fact: Lomuto's scheme is simpler but usually does more swaps.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the expected time of quickselect for finding the k-th smallest element?
fields.Hint: It recurses into only one side.
fields.Fact: The geometric series n + n/2 + n/4 and so on sums to about 2n.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Which selection algorithm finds the k-th smallest element in O(n) worst case time?
fields.Hint: Groups of five play a role.
fields.Fact: Blum, Floyd, Pratt, Rivest and Tarjan published it in 1973.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the worst case time of binary search on a sorted array of n elements?
fields.Hint: Each step discards half the range.
fields.Fact: About 30 comparisons suffice for a billion elements.

fields.Text: Binary search requires the array to be {{c1::sorted}}, or more generally a predicate that is {{c2::monotonic}} over the search range.
fields.Extra: Without that, discarding half the range is unsafe.
fields.Hint: What lets you rule out half the elements?
fields.Fact: Binary search on the answer applies the same idea to an abstract range of candidate values.

fields.Text: To avoid integer overflow, compute the binary search midpoint as {{c1::lo + (hi - lo) / 2}} instead of (lo + hi) / 2.
fields.Extra: int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
fields.Hint: The sum of two large indices can exceed the integer range.
fields.Fact: Joshua Bloch reported in 2006 that the JDK binary search had this overflow bug for years.

fields.Text: Python's bisect.bisect_left returns the {{c1::leftmost}} index at which x could be inserted while keeping the list sorted.
fields.Extra: bisect_right returns the position after any existing entries equal to x.
fields.Hint: With duplicates, it lands before them.
fields.Fact: The bisect module only works correctly on lists that are already sorted.

fields.Question: Which simple sort runs fastest on nearly sorted input?
fields.Hint: Few inversions mean few shifts.
fields.Fact: Timsort uses insertion sort for short runs.

fields.Question: At most how many swaps does selection sort make on n elements?
fields.Hint: One swap per pass.
fields.Fact: Few writes make it attractive when writing is expensive.

fields.Text: Introsort starts with quicksort and switches to {{c1::heapsort}} when the recursion depth exceeds a limit, guaranteeing O(n log n) worst case.
fields.Extra: Many C++ standard libraries implement std::sort this way.
fields.Hint: Which sort has a guaranteed bound and sorts in place?
fields.Fact: David Musser introduced introsort in 1997.

fields.Question: Which simple sort repeatedly swaps adjacent elements that are out of order?
fields.Hint: Large elements drift to the end.
fields.Fact: With an early exit when no swap occurs, it finishes in O(n) on sorted input.

fields.Text: Java's Arrays.sort for object arrays is a {{c1::stable}} adaptive merge sort, derived from Python's Timsort.
fields.Extra: For primitives it uses dual-pivot quicksort, where stability is not observable.
fields.Hint: Equal objects can be distinguished, so this matters.
fields.Fact: The Javadoc credits Tim Peters' list sort for Python.

fields.Text: To count occurrences of x in a sorted array, subtract the {{c1::leftmost}} insertion point from the {{c2::rightmost}} insertion point.
fields.Extra: In Python: bisect_right(a, x) - bisect_left(a, x).
fields.Hint: Two binary searches bound the run of equal values.
fields.Fact: This counts in O(log n) regardless of how many copies exist.

fields.Text: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has {{c1::optimal substructure}} and {{c2::overlapping subproblems}}.
fields.Extra: Without overlap, plain divide and conquer is enough.
fields.Hint: Solutions build from smaller solutions that repeat.
fields.Fact: Richard Bellman coined the term dynamic programming in the 1950s.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Hint: Recursion plus a cache.
fields.Fact: Python's functools.cache provides memoization in one decorator.

fields.Hint: Fill a table from small subproblems upward.
fields.Fact: Bottom-up order often allows keeping only the last row or two of the table.

fields.Question: Naive recursive Fibonacci runs in exponential time. Which simple bound is a valid upper bound on its running time?
fields.Hint: Each call makes two more calls.
fields.Fact: The tight bound is Theta(phi^n), where phi is the golden ratio, about 1.618.

fields.Question: What is the time of the standard DP for the longest common subsequence of strings of lengths m and n?
fields.Hint: One table cell per pair of prefixes.
fields.Fact: The diff tool is built on LCS style algorithms.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the time of the standard DP for 0/1 knapsack with n items and capacity W?
fields.Hint: One cell per item and capacity.
fields.Fact: 0/1 knapsack is NP-hard, so this bound is not polynomial in the input size.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: The O(nW) knapsack algorithm is {{c1::pseudo-polynomial}}: polynomial in the numeric value W, but exponential in the number of bits needed to write W.
fields.Extra: Doubling the bits of W squares its value.
fields.Hint: Look at how W is encoded in the input.
fields.Fact: Subset sum has a similar pseudo-polynomial DP.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the time of the standard DP for edit distance between strings of lengths m and n?
fields.Hint: Compare every prefix of one with every prefix of the other.
fields.Fact: The classic operations are insert, delete and substitute, as in Levenshtein distance.

fields.Question: What is the best known time for longest increasing subsequence using binary search over tails?
fields.Hint: Each element does one binary search.
fields.Fact: The simple DP takes O(n^2).

fields.Text: Greedy coin change can fail: with coins {1, 3, 4} and amount 6, greedy uses {{c1::3}} coins while the optimum is {{c2::2}} (3 + 3).
fields.Extra: Use DP for arbitrary coin systems.
fields.Hint: Greedy picks 4 first.
fields.Fact: Coin systems where greedy is always optimal are called canonical.

fields.Question: What problem does Kadane's algorithm solve in O(n)?
fields.Aliases:
maximum subarray
max subarray sum
largest sum contiguous subarray
fields.Hint: It tracks the best sum ending at each index.
fields.Fact: Jon Bentley popularized it in Programming Pearls, crediting Jay Kadane.

fields.Question: For maximizing the number of non-overlapping intervals, which interval does the greedy algorithm pick next?
fields.Aliases:
earliest end time
earliest finishing
smallest end
fields.Hint: Leave as much room as possible for the rest.
fields.Fact: Picking the shortest interval or earliest start can both fail.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Which algorithm design paradigm does Huffman coding use?
fields.Hint: It repeatedly merges the two least frequent symbols.
fields.Fact: David Huffman devised it in 1952 as a student at MIT.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: A greedy algorithm is correct when the problem has the {{c1::greedy choice property}} and optimal substructure.
fields.Extra: Proofs often use an exchange argument.
fields.Hint: A locally best choice must be extendable to a global optimum.
fields.Fact: Matroids give a general setting in which greedy algorithms are optimal.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Fractional knapsack is solved greedily by taking items in decreasing order of what?
fields.Aliases:
value to weight ratio
value/weight
value density
fields.Hint: Which items give the most per kilogram?
fields.Fact: The 0/1 version cannot be solved by this greedy rule.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: Backtracking builds candidates incrementally and {{c1::abandons}} a partial candidate as soon as it cannot lead to a valid solution.
fields.Extra: This pruning is what separates it from brute force enumeration.
fields.Hint: Undo the last choice and try another.
fields.Fact: The term was coined by D. H. Lehmer in the 1950s.

fields.Question: Which paradigm is the classic approach to the N-Queens problem?
fields.Hint: Place a queen, and retreat when stuck.
fields.Fact: The 8 queens puzzle has 92 solutions.

fields.Question: How many subsets does a set of n elements have?
fields.Hint: Each element is either in or out.
fields.Fact: Subset generation by backtracking therefore takes at least exponential time.

fields.Question: How many permutations do n distinct elements have?
fields.Hint: Choices shrink by one at each position.
fields.Fact: 10! is already 3,628,800.

fields.Question: Merge sort and quicksort are examples of which paradigm?
fields.Hint: Split, solve the parts, combine.
fields.Fact: Karatsuba's multiplication algorithm, found in 1960, was an early divide and conquer surprise.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the time of the Held-Karp bitmask DP for the traveling salesman problem on n cities?
fields.Hint: States are a subset plus a last city.
fields.Fact: It is far faster than checking all (n - 1)! tours, yet still exponential.

fields.Text: In the one dimensional 0/1 knapsack DP, iterate capacity {{c1::downward}} so each item is used at most once.
fields.Extra:
for w in range(W, wt - 1, -1):
    dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - wt] + val)
fields.Hint: Do not read a value you already updated for this item.
fields.Fact: Iterating upward instead gives the unbounded knapsack, where items can repeat.

fields.Question: Counting ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time follows which famous recurrence?
fields.Hint: The last move is either a 1 step or a 2 step.
fields.Fact: It runs in O(n) time with O(1) space keeping only two values.

fields.Question: Which paradigm solves matrix chain multiplication ordering in O(n^3)?
fields.Hint: Try every split point of every interval.
fields.Fact: The parenthesization changes the cost, not the product.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Text: On a sorted array, finding a pair with a given sum using {{c1::two pointers}} from both ends takes O(n) time and O(1) space.
fields.Extra: Move the left pointer up if the sum is too small, the right pointer down if too large.
fields.Hint: Start at the extremes and close in.
fields.Fact: On an unsorted array, a hash set gives O(n) time with O(n) space instead.

fields.Text: Longest substring without repeating characters is solved in O(n) with a {{c1::sliding window}} that shrinks from the left whenever a duplicate enters.
fields.Extra: A set or last-seen index map tracks the window.
fields.Hint: The window only moves forward.
fields.Fact: Each character enters and leaves the window at most once.

fields.Text: With prefix sums P where P[0] = 0 and P[i+1] = P[i] + a[i], the sum of a[i..j] inclusive is {{c1::P[j+1] - P[i]}}.
fields.Extra: Building P takes O(n); each range query is then O(1).
fields.Hint: Subtract everything before i.
fields.Fact: Two dimensional prefix sums answer rectangle queries the same way.

fields.Question: Which technique counts subarrays summing to k in O(n) even with negative numbers?
fields.Answer: Prefix sums with a hash map
fields.Aliases:
prefix sum and hash map
prefix sums
hash map of prefix sums
fields.Hint: Store how often each running total has appeared.
fields.Fact: A sliding window fails here because negatives break monotonicity.

fields.Text: To find the middle of a linked list in one pass, advance a {{c1::fast}} pointer two steps for each one step of a slow pointer.
fields.Extra: When the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow one is at the middle.
fields.Hint: Two speeds on one list.
fields.Fact: The same pointers detect cycles.

fields.Question: Which structure solves next greater element for every array index in O(n)?
fields.Hint: Pop smaller items when a bigger one arrives.
fields.Fact: Each index is pushed and popped at most once.

fields.Question: Which structure finds the maximum of every window of size k in O(n) total?
fields.Hint: Keep candidates in decreasing order and drop expired ones.
fields.Fact: Each index enters and leaves at most once, so the total work is linear.

fields.Question: Who posed the Dutch national flag problem of three-way partitioning?
fields.Hint: He also wrote Go To Statement Considered Harmful.
fields.Fact: Three-way partitioning makes quicksort efficient on inputs with many duplicate keys.

fields.Question: Which algorithm finds a majority element (more than n/2 occurrences) in O(n) time and O(1) space?
fields.Aliases:
Boyer-Moore voting algorithm
majority vote
Boyer Moore
fields.Hint: Keep one candidate and a counter.
fields.Fact: If no majority is guaranteed, a second pass must verify the candidate.

fields.Text: If every number appears twice except one, XOR of all elements gives the single one, because x ^ x = {{c1::0}} and x ^ 0 = x.
fields.Extra: XOR is commutative and associative, so order does not matter.
fields.Hint: Pairs cancel out.
fields.Fact: This uses O(n) time and O(1) space.

fields.Text: A positive integer n is a power of two exactly when {{c1::n & (n - 1)}} equals 0.
fields.Extra:
def is_power_of_two(n):
    return n > 0 and n & (n - 1) == 0
fields.Hint: Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and the zeros below it.
fields.Fact: Kernighan's bit counting trick uses the same expression to clear the lowest set bit.

fields.Question: What is the first step for merging overlapping intervals?
fields.Aliases:
sort by start time
sort intervals by start
fields.Hint: Overlaps become neighbours.
fields.Fact: After sorting, one linear scan merges everything, for O(n log n) total.

fields.Question: What is the technique of marking every land cell connected to a start cell, used to count islands in a grid?
fields.Hint: Like a paint bucket tool.
fields.Fact: Every cell is visited once, so it runs in O(rows x cols).

fields.Question: Rabin-Karp string matching relies on what technique?
fields.Hint: Update the window's fingerprint in O(1) as it slides.
fields.Fact: Hash matches are verified to rule out false positives.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: What is the time of Knuth-Morris-Pratt string matching for a text of length n and pattern of length m?
fields.Hint: The text pointer never moves backwards.
fields.Fact: KMP precomputes a prefix function telling how far to fall back on a mismatch.
fields.Source: Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/)

fields.Question: Deciding whether all courses with prerequisites can be finished is a cycle check usually solved with what?
fields.Hint: Courses are vertices, prerequisites are edges.
fields.Fact: If the topological order includes every course, the schedule is possible.

fields.Question: Besides a heap, which linear time technique solves top k frequent elements by grouping on counts?
fields.Hint: Frequencies are between 1 and n.
fields.Fact: Index buckets by count, then read from the highest bucket down.

fields.Text: Binary search on the answer, as in minimizing the largest load, works when feasibility is {{c1::monotonic}}: once a value works, every larger value also works.
fields.Extra: Search over candidate answers rather than array indices.
fields.Hint: Think of a yes or no test that flips once.
fields.Fact: Each step costs one feasibility check, giving O(check x log range).

fields.Text: An LRU cache with O(1) get and put combines a {{c1::hash map}} with a {{c2::doubly linked list}}.
fields.Extra: The map finds nodes; the list keeps recency order.
fields.Hint: One structure for lookup, one for order.
fields.Fact: Python's collections.OrderedDict has move_to_end, which makes a compact LRU.

fields.Text: Grouping anagrams uses a hash map keyed by each word's {{c1::sorted letters}} or its letter counts.
fields.Extra: Letter counts avoid the sort for short alphabets.
fields.Hint: All anagrams share a canonical form.
fields.Fact: Two strings are anagrams exactly when their character multisets match.

fields.Text: Removing duplicates in place from a sorted array uses a {{c1::slow}} write pointer and a fast read pointer.
fields.Extra: Runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space.
fields.Hint: One pointer reads, the other writes.
fields.Fact: The same pattern moves all zeros to the end of an array.

fields.Text: Longest palindromic substring can be found in O(n^2) by {{c1::expanding around each center}}, counting both single characters and gaps between characters.
fields.Extra: Manacher's algorithm achieves O(n).
fields.Hint: A palindrome is symmetric about its middle.
fields.Fact: A string of length n has 2n - 1 possible centers.

fields.Question: Which tree structure is the classic choice for autocomplete by prefix?
fields.Hint: Words sharing a prefix share a path.
fields.Fact: Each node represents a prefix rather than a whole key.

fields.Text: Cloning a graph with cycles needs a {{c1::hash map from original to copy}} so each vertex is copied once.
fields.Extra: BFS or DFS both work.
fields.Hint: Otherwise a cycle sends you round forever.
fields.Fact: The same map doubles as the visited set.

fields.Question: Word ladder (fewest single letter changes between words) is solved with which traversal?
fields.Hint: Every change costs the same.
fields.Fact: Bidirectional BFS from both ends often explores far fewer words.

fields.Question: Which technique picks k uniformly random items from a stream of unknown length in one pass?
fields.Hint: Replace a kept item with decreasing probability.
fields.Fact: With k = 1, the i-th item replaces the kept item with probability 1/i.

fields.Text: After Floyd's slow and fast pointers meet in a cyclic list, resetting one pointer to the {{c1::head}} and moving both one step at a time makes them meet at the cycle start.
fields.Extra: Distance from head to start equals distance from meeting point to start, modulo the cycle length.
fields.Hint: Restart one runner from the beginning.
fields.Fact: This finds the duplicate in an array of n + 1 values in 1..n without modifying it.
